Section I: Introduction to Buy & Build
Section I: Introduction to Buy & Build
Introduction
Add-on acquisitions as a key private equity strategy to build platform value through consolidation and multiple expansion
• Buy & Build strategies enhance value by combining scale, operational efficiency, and strategic synergies across complementary businesses
Key Drivers:

Platforms The initial, larger portfolio company serves as the structural and managerial foundation for subsequent acquisitions, provides the operational infrastructure required for integration and growth
Add-Ons Smaller companies acquired post-platform investment. These targets are typically valued at lower EBITDA multiples, creating potential for multiple arbitrage
Market Context Approximately 70% of PE buyouts involve at least one add-on, particularly in fragmented industries such as software, healthcare, and B2B services
Buy & Build Strategy When a platform completes four or more add-ons, the PE firm is executing a structured “Buy & Build” strategy aimed at market consolidation and operational leverage
Strategic Objectives To compound enterprise value by building scale, realizing cost and revenue synergies, and achieving valuation uplift as the integrated platform commands higher multiples
Section I: Introduction to Buy & Build
From Platform Acquisition to Exit
The execution of Buy & Build strategies
1. Equity: Initial At-risk capital with ownership and upside, but residual claim after debt
1. Platform Acquisition: A resilient, well-managed business is acquired to provide the operational backbone and governance framework for future expansion
2. Target Acquisition: The sponsor selectively acquires smaller, complementary businesses to add to the platform. These targets are typically purchased at lower valuation multiples

3. Integration: Alignment of the platform and acquired targets operationally, strategically, and culturally to unlock cost and revenue synergies. Combining complementary resources and expanding margins to drive sustained value creation

4. Exit: The private equity sponsor aims to sell or IPO the expanded platform at a higher valuation multiple than what was paid for the add-ons, capturing the uplift from scale, stability, and integration
By systematically acquiring, integrating, and scaling complementary businesses, private equity firms convert
fragmented markets into cohesive, higher-valued platforms

Add-on strategies enable platform companies to achieve inorganic growth by acquiring complementary businesses. This approach expands market presence, diversifies revenue streams, and strengthens competitive positioning, turning platforms into market leaders
through strategic consolidation rather than solely organic expansion

Section III: Value Creation Levers
Section III: Value Creation Levers
Revenue Synergies
Revenue synergies drive top-line growth in Buy & Build strategies
• Revenue synergies arise when the combined platform and add-ons can generate greater sales than each entity alone, through leveraging complementary products, customer bases, or market reach
Key Drivers:
Cross-Selling & Upselling Offering existing products to the acquired customer base or premium versions to platform clients
Market Expansion Entering new regions or customer segments through add-ons, accelerating international growth and reducing timeto-market for new offerings
Enhanced Value Proposition Creating a one-stop-shop offering that boosts client retention, pricing power, and overall share of customer wallet
Brand & Reputation Transfer
Using the platform’s established reputation to enhance credibility of smaller add-ons, improving conversion rates and customer trust
Innovation & Capability Synergies
Integrating specialized know-how, technology, or IP from add-ons to expand product range and strengthen competitive differentiation
Section III: Value Creation Levers
Cost Synergies
Cost synergies are the foundational levers of value creation in Buy & Build strategies

• Cost synergies attract greater scrutiny compared to revenue synergies owing to higher predictability, providing reliable bottom-line growth through operational improvements and ultimately margin expansion
Key Drivers:
Elimination of redundancies Streamlining/centralizing departments with similar functions within the combined enterprise, such as the back office
Economies of scale Pooling resources within the company to reduce unit fixed costs
Improved utilization Multifunctional capacity of existing resources leads to an increase in utilization rate
Parenting advantage Using the platform’s established structure to coordinate add-ons and introduce best practices, improving operational efficiency and aligning overall interests
Increased bargaining power Leveraging significant market share to negotiate favorable terms with suppliers

Section IV: The Value Creation Bridge
Section IV: The Value Creation Bridge
The Value Creation Bridge
Quantifying and visualizing value creation levers from add-on acquisitions
• The Value Creation Bridge breaks down total equity value creation into its key components showing where returns come from
• It is especially valuable in add-on acquisition analysis, as it highlights how value creation levers and integration effects compound across multiple acquisitions within a platform
1. Entry Equity: Initial equity value at acquisition, representing the platform’s baseline before integration effects
2. Revenue Synergies: Top-line growth achieved through cross-selling, new customers, and geographic expansion
3. Cost Synergies: Operational savings from integrating add-ons, sharing services, and reducing overhead costs
4. Multiple Arbitrage: Value created by buying add-ons and exiting the larger platform at a higher multiple
5. Exit Equity: Final equity value after capturing synergies and benefiting from multiple expansion

Section V: Integration Challenges
Section V: Integration Challenges
Integration Challenges
Acquiring firms often face challenges in realizing cost and revenue synergies when integrating an acquired company
• Estimating potential synergies accurately is difficult; ease and speed are often overestimated
• Integration risks often erode expected deal value
Potential Issues:
Strategic Misalignment Conflicting market positions and business models limit cross-selling potential and delay revenue synergy realization
Operational Integration Overlapping systems and fragmented processes extend integration timelines and erode expected cost savings
Culture Divergent leadership styles and corporate cultures undermine employee retention and morale
Regulatory Multi-jurisdictional antitrust reviews and tax complexities increase signing-to-closing risk and integration friction
Talent Key departures post-acquisition lead to loss of institutional knowledge and higher recruitment costs
